exercises.prompt: When you build a C# program, what does the C# compiler write to disk?

options.label: Machine code for the processor of the computer you built it on
options.feedback: Not yet — that would tie the program to one kind of processor. The translation to machine code happens later, on the machine that runs the program.

options.label: An assembly containing IL (intermediate language) and metadata
options.feedback: Yes. The compiler produces IL plus metadata describing every type; the runtime's JIT turns the IL into machine code when the program runs.

options.label: A copy of the source code, which the runtime interprets line by line
options.feedback: Not yet — the source is checked and compiled before anything runs. .NET does not interpret C# source.

options.label: Java bytecode, run by the Java virtual machine
options.feedback: Not yet — C# and Java share ideas, but .NET has its own instruction set (IL) and its own runtime (the CLR).

hints: There are two translations: one at build time and one at run time.
The file produced is called an assembly, even for a program.
exercises.solution: The compiler (Roslyn) checks the source and emits an **assembly**: a `.dll` holding IL for every method and metadata describing every type. When the program starts, the CLR loads the assembly and its JIT compiler translates each method's IL into machine code the first time the method runs. (Publishing with Native AOT is the exception: then everything is compiled to machine code ahead of time.)

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(typeof(long).FullName);
```

feedback.message: Not yet — `int` is 32 bits. How many bits does `long` have?
Not yet — the .NET type names say how many bits the integer has.

exercises.solution:
Every C# type keyword is an alias for a type in the `System` namespace. `long` is a 64-bit signed integer, so its .NET name is `System.Int64`, and `typeof(long).FullName` prints:

```text
System.Int64
```

exercises.prompt: You have a file `report.cs` containing top-level statements and no project file. With the .NET 10 SDK, which command builds and runs it?

options.label: `dotnet run report.cs`
options.feedback: Yes. Since .NET 10 the SDK builds a single file as a *file-based app*, caches the build, and runs it.

options.label: `csharp report.cs`
options.feedback: Not yet — there is no `csharp` command in the SDK; everything goes through the `dotnet` tool.

options.label: `dotnet new report.cs`
options.feedback: Not yet — `dotnet new` creates projects and files from templates; it does not run code.

options.label: `dotnet build` with no arguments
options.feedback: Not yet — with no arguments `dotnet build` looks for a project file in the current folder, and there is none.

hints: The command that both builds and runs is the same one you use for projects.
exercises.solution: `dotnet run report.cs` treats the file as a file-based app: the SDK creates a hidden project, compiles the file, caches the result and runs it. The same file can carry `#:package` and `#:property` directives, and `dotnet project convert report.cs` turns it into an ordinary project when it grows.

feedback.message: Not yet — a `TimeOnly` is a time of day, so it cannot go past 23:59. What happens at midnight?
Almost — the format `HH` always uses two digits.

hints: `TimeOnly.Add` wraps around, and `HH` pads to two digits.
exercises.solution:
22:30 plus 3 hours is 25:30, which is not a time of day. `TimeOnly.Add` wraps around midnight, giving 1:30 the next day, and the format `HH:mm` prints hours with two digits:

```text
01:30
```

exercises.prompt: A hospital is starting a new system in late 2026 that it expects to run, with security updates, for the next few years before its next planned upgrade. Which statements are true? (Choose all that apply.)

options.label: Even-numbered .NET releases such as .NET 10 are long-term support (LTS) releases
options.feedback: Yes. LTS releases get three years of fixes; even numbers have been LTS since .NET 6.

options.label: New code should target the Windows-only .NET Framework 4.8 because it is the most stable
options.feedback: Not yet — .NET Framework is maintained for existing software, but new development should use modern .NET, which is cross-platform and still evolving.

options.label: Each yearly .NET release comes with a new version of C#
options.feedback: Yes. .NET 10 brought C# 14, and .NET 11 brought C# 15.

options.label: Once compiled for .NET 10, a C# program can run only on the operating system it was built on
options.feedback: Not yet — an ordinary build produces IL, which runs on any operating system with the .NET 10 runtime.

hints: Think about the support policy: LTS versus STS.
What does an ordinary build produce, and where can it run?
exercises.solution: True: (a) and (c). .NET ships every November; even-numbered releases are LTS with three years of support, odd-numbered ones are STS with two. Each release brings a new C# version. (b) is false: .NET Framework is for maintaining older Windows software. (d) is false: IL in an assembly runs on any supported operating system that has the runtime; only Native AOT publishing produces an executable for one specific platform.
